entries.a60a77320901cae864e2211c670676079893ab61: <div sID="gen8986" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Esth.2" sID="Esth.2"/> <div eID="gen8986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8987" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8988" type="x-p"/> Two things are recorded in this chapter, which were working towards the deliverance of the Jews from Haman's conspiracy:—I. The advancement of Esther to be queen instead of Vashti. Many others were candidates for the honour (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.1-Esth.2.4">ver. 1-4</reference>); but Esther, an orphan, a captive-Jewess (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.5-Esth.2.7">ver. 5-7</reference>), recommended herself to the king's chamberlain first (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.8-Esth.2.11">ver. 8-11</reference>) and then to the king (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.12-Esth.2.17">ver. 12-17</reference>), who made her queen, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.18-Esth.2.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. II. The good service that Mordecai did to the king in discovering a plot against his life, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21-Esth.2.23">ver. 21-23</reference>.
entries.82c51d131b6b6c8c9c68de85415f39f2f2d93616: <div eID="gen8988" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8987" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Esther's Advancement; Esther Chosen Queen. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 514.)</title> <div sID="gen8989" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him, Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: <hi type="super">3</hi> And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given <hi type="italic">them:</hi> <hi type="super">4</hi> And let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti. And the thing pleased the king; and he did so. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">Now</hi> in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite; <hi type="super">6</hi> Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he brought up Hadassah, that <hi type="italic">is,</hi> Esther, his uncle's daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid <hi type="italic">was</hi> fair and beautiful; whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter. <hi type="super">8</hi> So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, <hi type="italic">which were</hi> meet to be given her, out of the king's house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best <hi type="italic">place</hi> of the house of the women. <hi type="super">10</hi> Esther had not showed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not show <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women's house, to know how Esther did, and what should become of her. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now when every maid's turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women, (for so were the days of their purifications accomplished, <hi type="italic">to wit,</hi> six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with <hi type="italic">other</hi> things for the purifying of the women;) <hi type="super">13</hi> Then thus came <hi type="italic">every</hi> maiden unto the king; whatsoever she desired was given her to go with her out of the house of the women unto the king's house. <hi type="super">14</hi> In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king's chamberlain, which kept the concubines: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name. <hi type="super">15</hi> Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her. <hi type="super">16</hi> So Esther was taken unto king Ahasuerus into his house royal in the tenth month, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Esther's feast; and he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when the virgins were gathered together the second time, then Mordecai sat in the king's gate. <hi type="super">20</hi> Esther had not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> showed her kindred nor her people; as Mordecai had charged her: for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him. <div eID="gen8989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8990" type="x-p"/> How God put down one that was high and mighty from her seat we read in the chapter before, and are now to be told how he exalted one of low degree, as the virgin Mary observes in her song (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.52">Luke i. 52</reference>) and Hannah before her, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4-1Sam.2.8">1 Sam. ii. 4-8</reference>. Vashti being humbled for her height, Esther is advanced for her humility. Observe, <div eID="gen8990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8991" type="x-p"/> I. The extravagant course that was taken to please the king with another wife instead of Vashti. Josephus says that when his anger was over he was exceedingly grieved that the matter was carried so far, and would have been reconciled to Vashti but that, by the constitution of the government, the judgment was irrevocable—that therefore, to make him forget her, they contrived how to entertain him first with a great variety of concubines, and then to fix him to the most agreeable of them all for a wife instead of Vashti. The marriages of princes are commonly made by policy and interest, for the enlarging of their dominions and the strengthening of their alliances; but this must be made partly by the agreeableness of the person to the king's fancy, whether she was rich or poor, noble or ignoble. What pains were taken to humour the king! As if his power and wealth were given him for no other end than that he might have all the delights of the sense wound up to the height of pleasurableness, and exquisitely refined, though at the best they are but dross and dregs in comparison with divine and spiritual pleasures. 1. All the provinces of his kingdom must be searched for fair young virgins, and officers appointed to choose them, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.3">v. 3</reference>. 2. A house (a seraglio) was prepared on purpose for them, and a person appointed to have the charge of them, to see that they were well provided for. 3. No less than twelve months was allowed them for their purification, some of them at least who were brought out of the country, that they might be very clean, and perfumed, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.12">v. 12</reference>. Even those who were the masterpieces of nature must yet have all this help from art to recommend them to a vain and carnal mind. 4. After the king had once taken them to his bed, they were made recluses ever after, except the king pleased at any time to send for them (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.14">v. 14</reference>); they were looked upon as secondary wives, were maintained by the king accordingly, and might not marry. We may see, by this instance, to what absurd practices those came who were destitute of divine revelation, and who, as a punishment for their idolatry, were given up to vile affections. Having broken through that law of creation which resulted from God's making man, they broke through another law, which was founded upon his making one man and one woman. See what need there was of the gospel of Christ to purify men from the lusts of the flesh and to reduce them to the original institution. Those that have <hi type="italic">learned Christ</hi> will think it <hi type="italic">a shame even to speak of such things as</hi> these which <hi type="italic">were done of them,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">in secret,</hi> but avowedly, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.12">Eph. v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen8991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8992" type="x-p"/> II. The overruling providence of God thus bringing Esther to be queen. Had she been recommended to Ahasuerus for a wife, he would have rejected the motion with disdain; but when she came in her turn, after several others, and it was found that though many of them were ingenious and discreet, graceful and agreeable, yet Esther excelled them all, way was made for her, even by her rivals, into the king's affections and the honours consequent thereupon. It is certain, as bishop Patrick says, that those who suggest that she committed a great sin to come at this dignity do not consider the custom of those times and countries. Every one that the king took to his bed was married to him, and was his wife of a lower rank, as Hagar was Abraham's; so that, if Esther had not been made queen, the sons of Jacob need not say that he <hi type="italic">dealt with their sister as with a harlot.</hi> Concerning Esther we must observe, <div eID="gen8992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8993" type="x-p"/> 1. Her original and character. (1.) She was one of the <hi type="italic">children of the captivity,</hi> a Jewess and a sharer with her people in their bondage. Daniel and his fellows were advanced in the land where they were captives; for they were of those whom God sent thither <hi type="italic">for their good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.24.5">Jer. xxiv. 5</reference>. (2.) She was an orphan; her father and mother were both dead (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.7">v. 7</reference>), but, when they had forsaken her, then the Lord took her up, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Ps. xxvii. 10</reference>. When those whose unhappiness it is to be thus deprived of their parents in their childhood yet afterwards come to be eminently pious and prosperous, we ought to take notice of it to the glory of that God, and his grace and providence, who has taken it among the titles of his honour to be a <hi type="italic">Father of the fatherless.</hi> (3.) She was a beauty, <hi type="italic">fair of form, good of countenance;</hi> so it is in the margin, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.7">v. 7</reference>. Her wisdom and virtue were her greatest beauty, but it is an advantage to be a diamond to be well set. (4.) Mordecai, her cousin-german, was her guardian, <hi type="italic">brought her up, and took her for his own daughter.</hi> The LXX. says that he designed to make her his wife; if that were so, he was to be praised that he opposed not her better preferment. Let God be acknowledged in raising up friends for the fatherless and motherless; let it be an encouragement to that pious instance of charity that many who have taken care of the education of orphans have lived to see the good fruit of their care and pains, abundantly to their comfort. Dr. Lightfoot thinks that this Mordecai is the same with that mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.2">Ezra ii. 2</reference>, who went up to Jerusalem with the first, and helped forward the settlement of his people until the building of the temple was stopped, and then went back to the Persian court, to see what service he could do them there. Mordecai being Esther's guardian or pro-parent, we are told, [1.] How tender he was of her, as if she had been his own child (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.11">v. 11</reference>): he walked before her door every day, to know how she did, and what interest she had. Let those whose relations are thus cast upon them by divine Providence be thus kindly affectioned to them and solicitous for them. [2.] How respectful she was to him. Though in relation she was his equal, yet, being in age and dependence his inferior, she honoured him as her father—<hi type="italic">did his commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.20">v. 20</reference>. This is an example to orphans; if they fall into the hands of those who love them and take care of them, let them make suitable returns of duty and affection. The less obliged their guardians were in duty to provide for them the more obliged they are in gratitude to honour and obey their guardians. Here is an instance of Esther's obsequiousness to Mordecai, that she did not <hi type="italic">show her people of her kindred,</hi> because Mordecai had charged her that she should not, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.10">v. 10</reference>. He did not bid her deny her country, nor tell a lie to conceal her parentage; if he had told her to do so, she must not have done it. But he only told her not to proclaim her country. All truths are not to be spoken at all times, though an untruth is not to be spoken at any time. She being born in Shushan, and her parents being dead, all took her to be of Persian extraction, and she was not bound to undeceive them. <div eID="gen8993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8994" type="x-p"/> 2. Her preferment. Who would have thought that a Jewess, a captive, and orphan, was born to be a queen, an empress! Yet so it proved. Providence sometimes <hi type="italic">raiseth up the poor out of the dust, to set them among princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1 Sam. ii. 8</reference>. (1.) The king's chamberlain honoured her (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.9">v. 9</reference>), and was ready to serve her. Wisdom and virtue will gain respect. Those that make sure of God's favour shall find favour with man too as far as it is good for them. All that looked upon Esther admired her (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">v. 15</reference>) and concluded that she was the lady that would win the prize, and she did win it. (2.) The king himself fell in love with her. She was not solicitous, as the rest of the maidens were, to set herself off with artificial beauty; she <hi type="italic">required nothing</hi> but just what was <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> for her (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">v. 15</reference>) and yet she was most acceptable. The more natural beauty is the more agreeable. <hi type="italic">The king loved Esther above all the women,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.17">v. 17</reference>. Now he needed not to make any further trials, or take time to deliberate; he is soon determined to <hi type="italic">set the royal crown upon her head, and make her queen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.17">v. 17</reference>. This was done in his seventh year (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.16">v. 16</reference>) and Vashti was divorced in his third year (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.3">ch. i. 3</reference>); so that he was four years without a queen. Notice is taken, [1.] Of the honours the king put upon Esther. He graced the solemnity of her coronation with a <hi type="italic">royal feast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.18">v. 18</reference>), at which perhaps Esther, in compliance with the king, made a public appearance, which Vashti had refused to do, that she might have the praise of obedience in the same instance in which the other incurred the blot of disobedience. He also granted a <hi type="italic">release to the provinces,</hi> either a remittance of the taxes in arrear or an act of grace for criminals; as Pilate, at the feast, released a prisoner. This was to add to the joy. [2.] Of the deference Esther continued to pay to her former guardian. She still <hi type="italic">did the commandment of Mordecai, as when she was brought up with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.20">v. 20</reference>. Mordecai sat <hi type="italic">in the king's gate;</hi> that was the height of his preferment: he was one of the porters or door-keepers of the court. Whether he had this place before, or whether Esther obtained it for him, we are not told; but there he sat contentedly, and aimed no higher; and yet Esther who was advanced to the throne was observant of him. This was an evidence of a humble and grateful disposition, that she had a sense of his former kindnesses and his continued wisdom. It is a great ornament to those that are advanced, and much to their praise, to remember their benefactors, to retain the impressions of their good education, to be diffident of themselves, willing to take advice, and thankful for it.
entries.d95055e43836cedd413cda0e9d3185a6461e0243: <div eID="gen8994" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mordecai's Discovery of a Plot. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen8995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king's gate, two of the king's chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king <hi type="italic">thereof</hi> in Mordecai's name. <hi type="super">23</hi> And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king. <div eID="gen8995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8996" type="x-p"/> This good service which Mordecai did to the government, in discovering a plot against the life of the king, is here recorded, because the mention of it will again occur to his advantage. No step is yet taken towards Haman's design of the Jews' destruction, but several steps are taken towards God's design of their deliverance, and this for one. God now gives Mordecai an opportunity of doing the king a good turn, that he might have the fairer opportunity afterwards of doing the Jews a good turn. 1. A design was laid against the king by two of his own servants, who sought <hi type="italic">to lay hands on him,</hi> not only to make him a prisoner, but to take away his life, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">v. 21</reference>. Probably they resented some affront which they thought he had given them, or some injury which he had done them. Who would be great, to be so much the object of envy? Who would be arbitrary, to be so much the object of ill-will? Princes, above any mortals, have their souls continually in their hands, and often go down <hi type="italic">slain to the pit,</hi> especially those who <hi type="italic">caused terror in the land of the living.</hi> 2. Mordecai got notice of their treason, and, by Esther's means, discovered it to the king, hereby confirming her in and recommending himself to the king's favour. How he came to the knowledge of it does not appear. Whether he overheard their discourse, or whether they offered to draw him in with them, so it was that <hi type="italic">the thing was known</hi> to him. This ought to be a warning against all traitorous and seditious practices: though men presume upon secresy, <hi type="italic">a bird of the air shall carry the voice.</hi> Mordecai, as soon as he knew it, caused it to be made known to the king, which ought to be an instruction and example to all that would be found good subjects not to conceal any bad design they know of against the prince or the public peace, for it is making a confederacy with public enemies. 3. The traitors were hanged, as they deserved, but not till their treason was, upon search, fully proved against them (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.23">v. 23</reference>), and the whole matter was recorded in the king's journals, with a particular remark that Mordecai was the man who discovered the treason. He was not rewarded presently, but a book of remembrance was written. Thus with respect to those who serve Christ, though their recompence is adjourned till the resurrection of the just, yet an account is kept of their <hi type="italic">work of faith and labour of love,</hi> which <hi type="italic">God is not unrighteous to forget,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>.  <chapter eID="Esth.2"/> <div eID="gen8996" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ac981943328ce0983be7614d382bb38469045e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4404"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.2.1-Esth.2.20">Es 2:1-20</reference>. Esther Chosen to Be Queen.</title> <div sID="gen6376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4404"/><hi type="bold">1-3. After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased--</hi>On recovering from the violent excitement of his revelry and rage, the king was pierced with poignant regret for the unmerited treatment he had given to his beautiful and dignified queen. But, according to the law, which made the word of a Persian king irrevocable, she could not be restored. His counsellors, for their own sake, were solicitous to remove his disquietude, and hastened to recommend the adoption of all suitable means for gratifying their royal master with another consort of equal or superior attractions to those of his divorced queen. In the despotic countries of the East the custom obtains that when an order is sent to a family for a young damsel to repair to the royal palace, the parents, however unwilling, dare not refuse the honor for their daughter; and although they know that when she is once in the royal harem, they will never see her again, they are obliged to yield a silent and passive compliance. On the occasion referred to, a general search was commanded to be made for the greatest beauties throughout the empire, in the hope that, from their ranks, the disconsolate monarch might select one for the honor of succeeding to the royal honors of Vashti. The damsels, on arrival at the palace, were placed under the custody of "Hege, the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women," that is, the chief eunuch, usually a repulsive old man, on whom the court ladies are very dependent, and whose favor they are always desirous to secure. <div eID="gen6376" type="x-p"/>
entries.b21a28d0f507873053b613b8bda564d32ccafd6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4405"/><div sID="gen6377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4405"/><hi type="bold">5. Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew--</hi>Mordecai held some office about the court. But his "sitting at the king's gate" (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Es 2:21</reference>) does not necessarily imply that he was in the humble condition of a porter; for, according to an institute of Cyrus, all state officers were required to wait in the outer courts till they were summoned into the presence chamber. He might, therefore, have been a person of some official dignity. This man had an orphan cousin, born during the exile, under his care, who being distinguished by great personal beauty, was one of the young damsels taken into the royal harem on this occasion. She had the good fortune at once to gain the good will of the chief eunuch [Es 2:9]. Her sweet and amiable appearance made her a favorite with all who looked upon her (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">Es 2:15</reference>, last clause). Her Hebrew name (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.7">Es 2:7</reference>) was Hadassah, that is, "myrtle," which, on her introduction into the royal harem, was changed to Esther, that is, the star Venus, indicating beauty and good fortune [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen6377" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8635aaa6c47a5ed85e9d3bcc316ff5b4f56b69e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4406"/><div sID="gen6378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4406"/><hi type="bold">11. Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women's house--</hi>The harem is an inviolable sanctuary, and what is transacted within its walls is as much a secret to those without as if they were thousands of miles away. But hints were given him through the eunuchs. <div eID="gen6378" type="x-p"/>
entries.c018ae02f9d7e935a6f5aeed752a300ce685d251: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4407"/><div sID="gen6379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4407"/><hi type="bold">12. Now when every maid's turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus--</hi>A whole year was spent in preparation for the intended honor. Considering that this took place in a palace, the long period prescribed, together with the profusion of costly and fragrant cosmetics employed, was probably required by state etiquette. <div eID="gen6379" type="x-p"/>
entries.3629785c85f277cff49d66958237b34e0361cc93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4408"/><div sID="gen6380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4408"/><hi type="bold">17. the king loved Esther above all the women--</hi>The choice fell on Esther, who found favor in the eyes of Ahasuerus. He elevated her to the dignity of chief wife, or queen. The other competitors had apartments assigned them in the royal harem, and were retained in the rank of secondary wives, of whom Oriental princes have a great number.<div eID="gen6380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he set the royal crown upon her head--</hi>This consisted only of a purple ribbon, streaked with white, bound round the forehead. The nuptials were celebrated by a magnificent entertainment, and, in honor of the auspicious occasion, "he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king." The dotation of Persian queens consisted in consigning to them the revenue of certain cities, in various parts of the kingdom, for defraying their personal and domestic expenditure. Some of these imposts the king remitted or lessened at this time. <div eID="gen6381" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc152013dae09be2e354bbc49b940ac0daed118b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4409"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.2.21-Esth.2.23">Es 2:21-23</reference>. Mordecai, Discovering a Treason, Is Recorded in the Chronicles.</title> <div sID="gen6382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4409"/><hi type="bold">21. In those days ... two of the king's chamberlains ... were wroth and sought to lay hand on the king, &c.--</hi>This secret conspiracy against the king's life probably arose out of revenge for the divorce of Vashti, in whose interest, and at whose instigation, these eunuchs may have acted. Through the vigilance of Mordecai, whose fidelity, however, passed unnoticed, the design was frustrated, while the conspirators were condemned to be executed and as the matter was recorded in the court annals, it became the occasion afterwards of Mordecai's preferment to the place of power and influence for which, in furtherance of the national interests of the Jews, divine providence intended him. <chapter eID="Esth.2"/>

entries.d9859c1ac526e56989f52b56792aabb5c50b3ff8: <div eID="gen15441" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15444" type="x-p"/> The counsellors advise that a selection of virgins should be made throughout the empire, out of whom the king should choose one to be queen in place of Vashti, <reference osisRef="Est.2.1-Est.2.4">Est 2:1-4</reference>. Account of Mordecai and his cousin Esther, <reference osisRef="Est.2.5-Est.2.7">Est 2:5-7</reference>. She is chosen among the young women, and is placed under the care of Hegai, the king's chamberlain, to go through a year's purification, <reference osisRef="Est.2.8-Est.2.11">Est 2:8-11</reference>. The manner in which these young women were introduced to the king, and how those were disposed of who were not called again to the king's bed, <reference osisRef="Est.2.12-Est.2.14">Est 2:12-14</reference>. Esther pleases the king, and is set above all the women; and he makes her queen in the place of Vashti, and does her great honor, <reference osisRef="Est.2.15-Est.2.20">Est 2:15-20</reference>. Mordecai, sitting at the king's gate, discovers a conspiracy formed against the king's life by two of his chamberlains; he informs the king, the matter is investigated, they are found guilty and hanged, and the transaction is recorded, <reference osisRef="Est.2.21-Est.2.23">Est 2:21-23</reference>.
entries.f62a7b699bb92975b56f5c9cef1a3d0cb47ff7ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15445" type="x-p"/> Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king - This was the usual way in which the harem or seraglio was furnished: the finest women in the land, whether of high or low birth, were sought out, and brought to the harem. They all became the king's concubines: but one was raised, as chief wife or sultana, to the throne; and her issue was specially entitled to inherit.
entries.d04ff2ac493dc9aa26186eb8fa3c415ba8988eee: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15446" type="x-p"/> Hege the king's chamberlain - הגא סריס המלך Hege seris hammelech, "Hege, the king's eunuch;" so the Septuagint, Vulgate, Targum, and Syriac. In the Eastern countries the women are intrusted to the care of the eunuchs only. <div eID="gen15446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15447" type="x-p"/> Let their things for purification be given them - תמרקיהן tamrukeyhen, their cosmetics. What these were we are told in <reference osisRef="Est.2.12">Est 2:12</reference>; oil of myrrh, and sweet odours. The myrrh was employed for six months, and the odours for six months more, after which the person was brought to the king. This space was sufficient to show whether the young woman had been chaste; whether she were with child or not, that the king might not be imposed on, and be obliged to father a spurious offspring, which might have been the case had not this precaution been used. <div eID="gen15447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15448" type="x-p"/> Instead of the oil or myrrh, the Targum says it was the oil of unripe olives which caused the hair to fall off, and rendered the skin delicate.
entries.552558bdfc4a2b82c5abf67b37e478a92c0bb070: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15449" type="x-p"/> Whose name was Mordecai - The Targum says, "He was the son of Jair, the son of Shimea, the son of Gera, the son of Kish." And "this was the same Shimea that cursed David; and whom David forbade Joab to slay because he saw, in the spirit of prophecy, that he was to be the predecessor of Esther and Mordecai; but when he became old, and incapable of having children, David ordered Solomon to put him to death.
entries.24c009f351c8ce6eb907b1c06fa5409e59052729: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15450" type="x-p"/> He brought up Hadassah - הדשה hadassah signifies a myrtle in Chaldee: this was probably her first or Babylonish name. When she came to the Persian court, she was called Esther, aster, or sitara, which signifies a star in Persian: the name is undoubtedly Persian. Esther was the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, and therefore must have been Mordecai's cousin, though the Vulgate and Josephus make her Mordecai's niece: but it is safest here to follow the Hebrew.
entries.0257ff9d02bca8a1273651c29220573b9024a87f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15451" type="x-p"/> The maiden pleased him - He conceived a partiality for her above the rest, probably because of the propriety of her deportment, and her engaging though unassuming manners. <div eID="gen15451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15452" type="x-p"/> Seven maidens - These were to attend her to the bath, to anoint and adorn her, and be her servants in general.
entries.7955648bbe1a75fbf5a3a27c8c4d9e255544eba0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15453" type="x-p"/> Esther had not showed her people - This might have prejudiced her with the king; for it was certainly no credit at the Persian court to be a Jew; and we shall find from the sequel that those who were in the Persian dominions were far from being reputable, or in a safe state. Besides, had her lineage been known, envy might have prevented her from ever having access to the king.
entries.3b1b2c7d98813b33f2c853597d6f37b27e5d7e7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen15453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15454" type="x-p"/> Six months with oil of myrrh - See on <reference osisRef="Est.2.3">Est 2:3</reference> (note). The reason of this purification seems not to be apprehended by any writer I have seen. The most beautiful of all the young virgins of all the provinces of Babylon were to be selected; and these were taken out of all classes of the people, indiscriminately; consequently there must have been many who were brought up in low life. Now we know that those who feed on coarse strong food, which is not easily digested, have generally a copious perspiration, which is strongly odorous; and in many, though in every respect amiable, and even beautiful, this odour is far from being pleasant. Pure, wholesome, easily digested, and nourishing aliment, with the frequent use of the hot bath, continued for twelve months, the body frequently rubbed with olive oil, will in almost every case remove all that is disagreeable of this kind. This treatment will give a healthy action to all the subcutaneous vessels, and in every respect promote health and comfort.
entries.6ca216268439f1f016631a2c83c054114ce91276: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15455" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever she desired - When any of the young women were called to go to the king, it appears that it was an ordinance that whatever kind of dress stuff, color, jewels, etc., they thought best to set off their persons, and render them more engaging, should be given them.
entries.5a79e7e2a5cf56e7947ebd2c28d6ffbe974121bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15456" type="x-p"/> She returned into the second house - This was the place where the king's concubines were kept. They went out no more, and were never given in marriage to any man, and saw the king's face no more unless specially called. <div eID="gen15456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15457" type="x-p"/> Custody of Shaashgaz - This is probably another Persian name; sheshkhunj, beardless, a proper epithet of a eunuch; or sestgunj, weak loins, for the same reason. Names of this kind at once show the reason of their imposition, by describing the state of the person.
entries.230403bf92c1692bb1484c4a6b95a87c47be5458: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15458" type="x-p"/> She required nothing - She left this entirely to her friend Hege, who seems to have been intent on her success. She therefore left her decorations to his judgment alone, and went in that dress and in those ornaments which he deemed most suitable.
entries.0c84c72afddf8bee348b48add710414d79903922: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15459" type="x-p"/> The tenth month - Tebeth - Answering to part of our December and January.
entries.fec747f5c9c5b919d55ed419f5565cc8bc5e8109: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15460" type="x-p"/> Set the royal crown upon her head - Made her what is now called in the East the Sultana, the queen. She was the mistress of all the rest of the wives, all of whom were obliged to pay her the most profound respect.
entries.2f566be5324079e790c63be912cafaa467ca1389: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen15460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15461" type="x-p"/> Made a release to the provinces - Remitted some kind of tribute or impost, in honor of Esther, at her coronation, as our kings generally do when they are crowned, ordering a discharge from prison of many who are confined for minor offenses. As it was the custom of the Persian kings to give their queens something like what is called with us the aurum reginae, "queen gold," which was a tenth of all fines, etc., above what was given to the king; (for they gave them such a city to buy them clothes, another for their hair, a third for their necklaces, a fourth for their pearls, etc.); it is probable that, on this occasion, Esther so wishing, he relieved those cities and provinces which had before paid this queen gold from all these expenses; and this would tend greatly to make the queen popular.
entries.ee7668fbcfd11c564e3b38c6174983fe008cc8d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen15461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15462" type="x-p"/> Mordecai sat in the kings gate - Mordecai might have been one of the officers of the king, as the gate was the place where such usually attended to await the king's call. It is not likely that he was the porter; had he been only such, Haman could have removed him at once. <div eID="gen15462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15463" type="x-p"/> Two of the king's chamberlains - Eunuchs. Why they conspired against the life of the king, we are not informed. The Targum says that they found out that Esther had intended to use her influence with the king to get them removed from their office, and Mordecai put in their place; therefore they determined to poison Esther, and slay the king in his bedchamber. It is very likely that they were creatures of Haman, who probably affected the kingdom, and perhaps were employed by him to remove the king, and so make his way open to the throne.
entries.66ed9c5d01baeac8ae4a6d7fe83d1f4383fca25e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15464" type="x-p"/> Was known to Mordecai - Josephus says that a Jew, named Barnabasus, overheard the plot, told it to Mordecai, Mordecai to Esther, and Esther to the king, in Mordecai's name; and he was registered as the discoverer.
entries.21a9bc81b94fa0d5f4b5ee043cc249b0b0a69e53: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen15464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15465" type="x-p"/> It was found out - It was proved against them, in consequence of which they were hanged. Perhaps the words ויתלו על עץ vaiyittalu al ets, they were hung upon wood or a tree, may refer to their being impaled. A pointed stake is set upright in the ground, and the culprit is taken, placed on the sharp point, and then pulled down by his legs till the stake that went in at the fundament passes up through the body and comes out by the side of the neck. A most dreadful species of punishment, in which revenge and cruelty may glut the utmost of their malice. The culprit lives a considerable time in excruciating agonies. <div eID="gen15465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15466" type="x-p"/> It has been observed that the name of God does not once occur in this book. This is true of the Hebrew text, and all translations from it; but in the Septuagint we find the following words, in <reference osisRef="Est.2.20">Est 2:20</reference>, after, Esther had not showed her kindred: Οὑτως γαρ ενετειλατο αυτῃ Μαρδοχαιος, φοβεισθαι τον Θεον, και ποιειν τα προσταγματα αυτου, καθως ην μετ' αυτου; "For so Mordecai had charged her to fear God, and to keep his commandments, as she did when with him." This, as far as the Septuagint is concerned, takes away the strange reproach from this book. It must be owned that it was not because there were not many fair opportunities that the sacred name has not been introduced.  <chapter eID="Esth.2"/> <div eID="gen15466" type="x-p"/>

entries.77ab2ac018e7c11f23cbe047808e41f18c21f9a5: <div eID="gen6705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Elevation of Esther to the Throne - Esther 2</title> <div sID="gen6706" type="x-p"/> Service Rendered by Mordochai to the King <div eID="gen6706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6707" type="x-p"/> When the wrath of King Ahashverosh was appeased, and he remembered his harsh treatment of Vashti, his courtiers proposed that he should send to fetch fair young virgins from all parts of his realm to the house of the women in Susa, that he might choose a new queen from among them. This proposal pleasing the king, was acted upon (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.1-Esth.2.4">Est 2:1-4</reference>). In the fortress of Susa, however, there dwelt one of the Jews who had been carried into captivity from Jerusalem, and whose name was Mordochai. This man had brought up Esther, his uncle’s daughter, as his own child (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.5-Esth.2.7">Est 2:5-7</reference>). When, then, in pursuance with the king’s commands, many maidens were gathered together in Susa, Esther also was brought into the king’s house, and found favour with the keeper of the women while, according to order, she was going through a course of purification and anointing (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.8-Esth.2.14">Est 2:8-14</reference>). Then her turn came to be brought before the king, she found favour in his sight above all the other maidens, and was chosen by him to be queen in the place of Vashti. By Mordochai’s command, however, she disclosed her race and lineage to no one (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.15-Esth.2.20">Est 2:15-20</reference>). At the same time two courtiers conspired against the life of the sovereign. Their conspiracy being discovered by Mordochai, was by him revealed to Esther, who gave information of it to the king, whereupon the matter was investigated, and found to have been correctly stated. The offenders were punished, and the event duly registered in the chronicles of the kingdom. <div eID="gen6707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6708" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.1-Esth.2.4">Est 2:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen6708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6709" type="x-p"/> When, after these things, the wrath of King Ahashverosh was laid (שׁך, from שׁכך, to be sunk, spoken of wrath to be laid), he remembered Vashti and what she had done, and what was decreed against her (גּזר, to determine, to decree irrevocably; comp. גּזרה, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference>); a desire for reunion with her evidently making itself felt, accompanied perhaps by the thought that she might have been too harshly treated. To prevent, then, a return of affection for his rejected wife ensuing, - a circumstance which might greatly endanger all who had concurred in effecting her repudiation, - the servants of the king, i.e., the court officials who were about him, said: “Let there be young maidens, virgins fair to look on, sought for the king.” בּתוּלות, virgins, is added to נערות, the latter word signifying merely young women of marriageable age. Est 2:3. “And let the king appoint (ויפקד is the continuation of יבקּשׁוּ) officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together every virgin who is fair to look on to the citadel of Susa, to the house of the women, unto the hand of Hega the king’s eunuch, the keeper of the women, and let them appoint their things for purification; and let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti.” To the hand of Hega, i.e., to his care and superintendence, under which, as appears from <reference osisRef="Esth.2.12">Est 2:12</reference>, every maiden received into the house of the women had to pass a year before she was brought before the king. Hega (called Hegai, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.8">Est 2:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">Est 2:15</reference>) was an eunuch, the keeper of the women, i.e., superintendent of the royal harem. ונתון is the <hi type="italic">infin. abs</hi>., used instead of the <hi type="italic">verb. fin</hi>. to give prominence to the matter: let them appoint. תּמרקום, from מרק, to rub, to polish, signifies purification and adornment with all kind of precious ointments; comp. Est 2:12. This speech pleased the king, and he acted accordingly.
entries.fcb6cf9c1f6aeda240b62379366b86aadb6b8f20: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.5-Esth.2.7">Est 2:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen6709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6710" type="x-p"/> Before relating how this matter was carried into execution, the historian introduces us to the two persons who play the chief parts in the following narrative. Est 2:5. There was (dwelt) in the citadel of Susa a Jew of the name of Mordochai (מרדּכי, in more correct editions מרדכי), the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite (ימיני אישׁ like <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>). Jair, Shimei, and Kish can hardly mean the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of Mordochai. On the contrary, if Jair were perhaps his father, Shimei and Kish may have been the names of renowned ancestors. Shimei was probably the son of Gera, well known to us from the history of David, 2Sa 16:5. and 1Ki 2:8, 1Ki 2:36., and Kish the father of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1Ch 8:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>; for in genealogical series only a few noted names are generally given; comp., e.g., <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19">1Ch 9:19</reference>; 1Ch 6:24. Upon the ground of this explanation, Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xi. 6) makes Esther of royal descent, viz., of the line of Saul, king of Israel; and the Targum regards Shimei as the Benjamite who cursed David. The name Mordochai occurs in Ezr 2:2 and <reference osisRef="Neh.7.7">Neh 7:7</reference> as that of some other individual among those who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel, but can hardly be connected with the Persian <hi type="italic">mrdky</hi>, little man. Aben Ezra, Lightfoot, and others, indeed, are of opinion that the Mordochai of the present book really came up with Zerubbabel, but subsequently returned to Babylon. Identity of name is not, however, a sufficient proof of identity of person. The chronological statement, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.6">Est 2:6</reference> : who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been carried away with Jeconiah, king of Judah, etc., offers some difficulty. For from the captivity of Jeconiah in the year 599 to the beginning of the reign of Xerxes (in the year 486) is a period of 113 years; hence, if the אשׁר is referred to Mordochai, he would, even if carried into captivity as a child by then, have reached the age of from 120 to 130 years, and as Esther was not made queen till the seventh year of Xerxes (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.16">Est 2:16</reference>), would have become prime minister of that monarch at <hi type="italic">about</hi> the age of 125. Rambach, indeed, does not find this age incredible, though we cannot regard it as probable that Mordochai should have become minister at so advanced an age.<note placement="foot">Baumg. aptly remarks, l.c., p. 125: <hi type="italic">Etsi concedendum est, non esse contra naturam, si Mordechaeus ad illam aetatem pervenerit, et summa hac constitutus senectute gravissimis negotiis perficiendis par fuerit, tamen est hoc rarissimum et nisi accedit certum testimonium, difficile ad credendum</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen6710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6711" type="x-p"/> On this account Clericus, Baumgarten, and others refer the relative אשׁר to the last name, Kish, and understand that he was carried away with Jeconiah, while his great-grandson Mordochai was born in captivity. In this case Kish and Shimei must be regarded as the great-grandfather and grandfather of Mordochai. We grant the possibility of this view; nevertheless it is more in accordance with the Hebrew narrative style to refer אשׁר to the chief person of the sentence preceding it, viz., Mordochai, who also continues to be spoken of in Est 2:7. Hence we prefer this reference, without, however, attributing to Mordochai more than 120 years of age. For the relative clause: who had been carried away, need not be so strictly understood as to assert that Mordochai himself was carried away; but the object being to give merely his origin and lineage, and not his history, it involves only the notion that he belonged to those Jews who were carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar with Jeconiah, so that he, though born in captivity, was carried to Babylon in the persons of his forefathers. This view of the passage corresponds with that formerly presented by the list of the grandchildren and great-grandchildren of Jacob who went down with him to Egypt; see the explanation of the passage in question.<note placement="foot">Baumgarten also considers this view admissible, rightly remarking, p. 127: <hi type="italic">Scriptoribus sacris admodum familiare est singulos homines non per se et sepositos spectare, sed familias et gentes ut corpora quasi individua complecti, ita ut posteri majorum personis quasi contenti et inclusi, majores vero in posteris ipsi subsistere et vivere existimentur. Ex hac ratione Mordechaeus captus esse dici potest, quamvis ipse satis diu post Jechoniae tempora ex iis, qui a Nebucadnezaro abducti sunt, natus fuerit</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen6711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6712" type="x-p"/> Est 2:7. Mordochai was אמן, keeper, bringer up, i.e., foster-father, to Hadassh (אמן constructed as a participle with את). הדסּה means a myrtle (הדס in the Shemitish), like the Greek name Μυρτία, Μυῤῥίνη. “That is Esther,” the queen known by the name of Esther. The name אסתּר is the Old-Persian <hi type="italic">stara</hi> with א prosthetic, and corresponds with the Greek ἀστήρ, star, in modern Persian <hi type="italic">sitareh</hi>. She was בּת־דּדו, daughter of his father’s brother, and adopted by Mordochai after the death of her parents; we are told, moreover, that she had a fine figure and beautiful countenance. Her father, whose name, according to <reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">Est 2:15</reference>, was Abihail, was uncle to Mordochai, and hence Esther was his cousin.
entries.14d7df3ece8c4ad0dbbc5897013516e445bcbf49: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.8-Esth.2.9">Est 2:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen6712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6713" type="x-p"/> When, then, the king’s commandment and decree was heard, i.e., proclaimed throughout the kingdom, and many maidens gathered together in Susa, Esther also was received into the royal harem, under the keeping of Hegai. The maiden pleased him and won his favour (חסד נשׂא, to bear away love, i.e., to obtain favour, synonymous with חן נשׂא, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">Est 2:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.5.2">Est 5:2</reference>). וגו ויבהל, and he hastened to give her her ointments for purification, and the seven maidens appointed to her from the king’s house. The infinitives להּ לתת are, according to the Aramaean idiom, placed after their objects and dependent on יבהל. On תּמרוּקים, see on Est 2:3. מנות, portions, are here portions of food, as in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Est 9:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">Est 9:22</reference>, and 1Sa 1:4. The seven maidens (הנּערות with the article) are the maids appointed to wait upon a young virgin selected for the king. The participle ראיּות: chosen for a particular purpose-in the Talmud and rabbinical Hebrew ראוּי, <hi type="italic">dignus, decens, conveniens,</hi> - occurs only here. ישׁנּה, he changed her and her maids into the best of the house of the women, i.e., he took them out of the ordinary rooms and placed them in the best apartments, probably in the state-rooms, where those who were accustomed to be brought to the king used to dwell.
entries.4fd63595d3f539f94486412b604ffec06ff306a9: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.10-Esth.2.11">Est 2:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen6713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6714" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.10">Est 2:10</reference> contains a supplementary remark. This kind and respectful treatment was shown to Esther, because, in obedience to Mordochai’s command, she had not shown her people nor her kindred, i.e., her Jewish extraction; for a Jewish maiden would hardly have experienced such friendly usage. <reference osisRef="Esth.2.11">Est 2:11</reference> also contains an additional notice, prefixed here to enable what follows to be rightly understood, and repeated in another connection <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Est 2:19</reference>, and on several other occasions: Mordochai walked every day before the court or enclosure of the women’s house, to know the welfare (שׁלום) of Esther and what became of her (בּה יעשׂה, properly, what was done to her). Hence Mordochai was in constant communication with Esther. How this communication was effected is not more particularly stated; probably by means of the maids appointed to wait on her. Jewish expositors are of opinion, that Mordochai held high office, and that having consequently free access to the royal palace, he could easily find the means of communicating with his relative. <div eID="gen6714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6715" type="x-p"/> Before relating the appearance of Esther before the king, the narrator more particularly describes in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.12-Esth.2.14">Est 2:12-14</reference> the preparations for this event, and how Esther behaved with respect to them.
entries.79f4f3b9a1a944d230f11d7ac04eef8511020f0a: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.12-Esth.2.13">Est 2:12-13</reference> “When every maid’s turn came (i.e., at every time that any maid’s turn came) to go in to King Ahashverosh, after the time when it had been done to her twelve months according to the law of the women - for thus were the days of their purification accomplished: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with balsam and ointments of purification for women - and the maiden came to the king, all that she desired was given her to go with her out of the women’s house unto the king’s house.” תּור, turn in succession, used only here and Est 2:15. The turn to go in unto the king did not come to any maid until וגו היות מקּץ, at the end of the time when it had been done to her according to the law ... This time lasted twelve months after her reception into the house of the women; and the law of the women, according to which it was done to her, was, that she should be purified for six months with oil of myrrh, and as long with בּשׂמים, sweet odours and other ointments. בּאה הנּערה וּבזה (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.13">Est 2:13</reference>) forms the continuation of the antecedent clause commencing with כּהנּיע, or, to speak more correctly, of a second antedecent with which the conclusion כּל־אשׁר את is connected. Some expositors understand בּזה, with the lxx, of the time: <hi type="italic">illo sc. tempore;</hi> others of the condition: <hi type="italic">hoc modo ornata or ea lege</hi> (Cler.), and therefore as parallel in meaning with the כּן of Est 4:16. Either view is admissible and suits the sense, but the latter is more in harmony with the parallel passage <reference osisRef="Esth.4.16">Est 4:16</reference>, and therefore preferable. All that was to be given her, can only relate to ornaments and jewels, which were to be given that each might appear before the king adorned and dressed after her own taste.
entries.a04de663ed0b6109112f8ee564ec5065f44d9e50: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.14">Est 2:14</reference> <div eID="gen6715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6716" type="x-p"/> In the evening she went (to the king), and on the morrow she returned to the women’s house, a second (time) to the hand (under the keeping of) Shaashgaz, the king’s chamberlain, who kept the concubines; she came no more to the king, except the king delighted in her and she were called by name, i.e., specially. שׁני instead of שׁנית, like Neh 3:30.
entries.60d2a49190ba90f7f865e4bea16ea86187e6b6fb: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.15">Est 2:15</reference> <div eID="gen6716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6717" type="x-p"/> When Esther’s turn came to go in unto the king, she required nothing (to take with her, see <reference osisRef="Esth.2.13">Est 2:13</reference>) but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain appointed (hence as not concerned to please the king by special adornment), and she obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her, namely, by her modesty and humility. On חן נשׂא, see remarks on Est 2:9.
entries.5e6be2b91876bded327852964ba6d8099fedbefb: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.16">Est 2:16</reference> <div eID="gen6717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6718" type="x-p"/> She was taken into the king’s house (מלכוּת בּית instead of המּלך בּית, the palace of the kingdom, the royal residence) in the tenth month, i.e., the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.
entries.b0261083a6a675c84ffc0722cb45a837fa67c5df: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.17">Est 2:17</reference> <div eID="gen6718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6719" type="x-p"/> And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; and he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. The meaning evidently is, that the king, immediately after their first meeting, bestowed his affections upon Esther in preference to all the women and maidens, and chose her queen.
entries.c1eafc40b7943679831a8a614cf40ab5e6152b24: <reference osisRef="Esth.2.18">Est 2:18</reference> <div eID="gen6719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6720" type="x-p"/> To celebrate Esther’s elevation to the crown, the king made a great feast, called Esther’s feast, to all his princes and servants, and granted release to the provinces. The <hi type="italic">verbale Hiph</hi>. הנחה is translated in the lxx ἄφεσις, Vulg. <hi type="italic">requies</hi>, and understood either of a remission of taxes or a remission of labour, a holiday. Although the Chald. understands it of a remission of taxes, yet the use of the verb עשׂה rather favours the latter meaning, viz., the appointment of a holiday, on which there would be arresting from labour. Finally, he gave gifts with royal munificence משׂאת like <reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">Jer 40:5</reference>; המּלך כּיד like Est 1:7. - It seems strange that a period of four years should intervene between the repudiation of Vashti in the third year of Ahashverosh and the elevation of Esther in the seventh, an interval whose length cannot be adequately accounted for by the statements of the present book. Only a few days could have elapsed between the disgrace of Vashti and the time when the king remembered her; for this took place, we are told, when the king’s wrath was appeased. The proposal to collect virgins from all parts of his kingdom to Susa was then immediately made. Now, if the carrying out of this proposal took half a year, and the preparation of the virgins by anointing, etc., lasted a year, Esther, even if her turn to go in unto the king had not come for six months, might have been made queen two years after the repudiation of Vashti. As she obtained the favour of Hegai immediately upon her reception into the women’s house, so that he hastened her purifications (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.9">Est 2:9</reference>), she would not be brought before the king among the last, but would rather be one of the first to go in. The long interval which elapsed between the repudiation of Vashti and the elevation of Esther, can only be satisfactorily explained by the history of the reign of Xerxes; in fact, by the circumstance that his campaign against Greece took place during this time. <div eID="gen6720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6721" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19-Esth.2.23">Est 2:19-23</reference> relate the intervention of an incident of great importance in the subsequent development of the narrative. When virgins were for the second time gathered together, two courtiers were incensed with the king, and sought to lay hands upon him. This thing was known to Mordochai, who sat in the gate of the palace and kept up a constant communication with Esther even after she became queen, and by him communicated to her, that she might bring it to the knowledge of the king. The matter being investigated and found to have been truly reported, the offenders were punished, and an entry of the particulars made in the chronicles of the kingdom. The words “when virgins were assembled for the second time,” which serve to define the time when the conspiracy of the two courtiers took place, as is obvious from the circumstance that ההם בּיּמים, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Est 2:21</reference>, refers to בת בּהקּבץ, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Est 2:19</reference>, are obscure. The obscurity lies in the fact that no reason for assembling virgins can be perceived, after the choice of Ahashverosh had fallen upon Esther. The sentence שׁנית בּתוּלות וּבהקּבץ unmistakeably corresponds with נערות וּבהקּבץ of v. 8. This was already rightly perceived by Grotius, who, however, wrongly infers: <hi type="italic">est</hi> ἐπάνοδος (<hi type="italic">retrogressio</hi>), <hi type="italic">referendum enim hoc ad illa quae supra</hi>, ii. 2. This is, however, not only incompatible with שׁנית, but also with the circumstance that, according to the correct understanding of the sentences in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.21">Est 2:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.2.22">Est 2:22</reference>, Esther was then already queen, and Mordochai was sitting in the gate of the king’s palace, and thence keeping up communication with her; while as long as Esther was in the women’s house preparing for her interview with the king, under the guardianship of Hegai, he walked day by day before the court of the women’s house (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.11">Est 2:11</reference>). Still less admissible is the view of Drusius, received by Bertheau, that the gathering of the virgins for the second time is to be understood from the circumstance, that after going in to the king, they had to go into the second house of the women, under the stricter guardianship of Shaashgaz (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.14">Est 2:14</reference>). For, being no longer בּתוּלות, but פּילגשׁים (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.14">Est 2:14</reference>), their reception into the house of the concubines could not be called a second gathering together, since as virgins they were formerly in a different house. The only explanation of the שׁנית left us is the view, that even after the choice of Esther to be queen, a second gathering together of virgins actually took place; for this, as C. a Lapide remarks, is what the words undoubtedly declare. The matter itself was in accordance with the prevailing custom of polygamy, which kings carried to such an extent, that, as C. a Lapide points out, Solomon, e.g., had 700 wives and 300 concubines, i.e., <hi type="italic">secondarias uxores</hi>. From וּמרדּכי, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Est 2:19</reference>, onwards, explanatory circumstantial clauses follow: “The Mordochai sat in the king’s gate” introduces the parenthetical sentence, “Esther had not yet showed her kindred and her people (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.2.10">Est 2:10</reference>), as Mordochai had charged her; for Esther did the commandment of Mordochai as when she was under his care;” i.e., Esther obeyed, after her elevation to be queen, the command of Mordochai not to make her Jewish descent known, as she had formerly done while she was yet his foster-daughter. אמנה, care, education, is a substantive derived from אמן. <div eID="gen6721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6722" type="x-p"/> The definition of time in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Est 2:19</reference> is again take up by the words: in those days; then the explanatory clause, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.20">Est 2:20</reference>, is repeated; and after this we are informed what it was that had then occurred. In those days Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s courtiers, who were the threshold-keepers (palace-watchers, lxx ἀρχισωματοφύλακες), were wroth, and sought to lay hands on King Ahashverosh, i.e., to slay him. Est 2:22. This thing was known to Mordochai, and by him communicated to Esther, who told it, in Mordochai’s name, to the king. Est 2:23. The matter was investigated (sc. by the king), and found out, sc. as Mordochai had testified. The two criminals were hanged on a tree, i.e., impaled on a stake, a sort of crucifixion, - see rem. on <reference osisRef="Esth.6.11">Est 6:11</reference>, - and the circumstance entered in the book of the chronicles, i.e., the chronicles of the kingdom. המּלך לפני, before the king, i.e., in his presence, immediately after sentence had been passed by a court over which the monarch presided. Haman’s Elevation and His Design against the Jews - <reference osisRef="Esth.3.1-Esth.3.15">Est 3:1-15</reference> <div eID="gen6722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6723" type="x-p"/> King Ahashverosh promoted Haman the Agagite above all the princes about him, and commanded all his servants to fall down before him. This mark of reverence was refused by Mordochai the Jew from religious scruples. When intelligence of this was brought to Haman, he sought to obtain the extermination of the Jews throughout the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.1-Esth.3.6">Est 3:1-6</reference>). The twelfth month was appointed by the casting of lots for this purpose; and Haman, by exciting the suspicion of the king against the Jews as an exclusive and law-opposing people, obtained from him an edict to this effect (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.7-Esth.3.11">Est 3:7-11</reference>), and sent it, by letters sealed with the king’s seal, by the hand of messengers into all the provinces of the kingdom in the first month, that they might be ready to carry it into execution in the twelfth month; whereat the city of Susa was much perplexed (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.12-Esth.3.15">Est 3:12-15</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.2"/> <div eID="gen6723" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. II.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AFter these things when the wrath of king Aha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suerus was appeased, he remembred <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With grief and shame, that in his Wine and Rage, he had so severely punished, and so irrevocably rejected so beautiful and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sireable a Person, and that for so small a provocation, to which she was easily led by the modesty of her Sex, and by the Laws and Customs of <ns0:hi>Persia.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Then said the kings servants <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who for their own Interests were obliged to quiet the Kings Mind, and procure him another amiable Consort.</ns0:note>, that ministred un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him, Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And let the king appoint Officers in all the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>unto the hand.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> unto the custody of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Hegai<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> v.</ns0:hi> 8.</ns0:note> Hege the kings chamberlain, keeper of the women <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either 1 Of the Virgins, who are oft called <ns0:hi>Women,</ns0:hi> as here <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11, 12. and elsewhere. So it is a Synecdoche. Or 2. Of all the Women, both Virgins and Concubines: only the Virgins he himself took care of, as requiring more care and caution, and the Concubines he committed to <ns0:hi>Shaashgaz, ver.</ns0:hi> 14. his Deputy.</ns0:note>, and let their things for purification <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To cleanse them from all impurities and indecencies, to a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />noint, and perfume, and adorn, and every way prepare them for the Kings presence and service: for the legal purifications of the Jews he never regarded.</ns0:note> be given <ns0:hi>them.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And let the maiden which pleaseth the king, be queen instead of Vashti. And the thing pleased the king, and he did so.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:hi>Now</ns0:hi> in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Kin. 24. 15. 2 Chr. 36. 10, Jer. 24. 1.</ns0:note> Who <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This may be referred either 1. To <ns0:hi>Kish, Mordecai</ns0:hi>'s Grand-Father last mentioned; or 2. To <ns0:hi>Mordecai,</ns0:hi> who <ns0:hi>was then carried away</ns0:hi> either 1. In the Loins of his Parents, in which sense <ns0:hi>Levi</ns0:hi> is said to <ns0:hi>be tithed in Abraham,</ns0:hi> Heb. 7. and as those persons named <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 2. are said to have <ns0:hi>been carried away by Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> Ezra 2. 1. which is not true of the most of them in their own per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons, but only as in their Fathers Loins. Or 2. In his own per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son: and then indeed he was a man of more than ordinary years. But of that see the notes on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 1.</ns0:note> had been carried away from Jerusalem, with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And he <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>nou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rished.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> brought up Hadassah (that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Esther <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Hadassah</ns0:hi> was her Hebrew name before her marriage; and she was called <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> by the King after it.</ns0:note>) his uncles daughter, for she had neither father nor mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, and the maid <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>fair of form, and good of countinance.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> fair and beautiful, whom Mordecai (when her father and mother were dead) took for his own daughter.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 So it came to pass, when the kings command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>taken,</ns0:hi> and that by force, as that word oft signifies: So great was the power and Tyranny of the Persian Kings, that they could and did take what persons they liked to their own use.</ns0:note> also unto the kings house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the maiden pleased him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Partly because she was very beautiful, and therefore he suppo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed she would be very acceptable to the King; which would be his advantage; and partly by the Divine Power, which moveth the hearts of men which way he pleaseth.</ns0:note>, and she obtained kindness of him, and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>her por<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, <ns0:hi>which were</ns0:hi> meet to be given her, out of the kings house, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>he changed her.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> he preferred her and her maids unto the best <ns0:hi>place</ns0:hi> of the house of the women.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:378" />10 Esther had not shewed her people, nor her kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Lest the knowledge hereof should either make her contempti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble or odious; or bring some inconvenience to the whole nation, as things might happen. But there was also an hand of God in cau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing this to be concealed for the better accomplishment of that which he designed, though <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi> was ignorant of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the womens house, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to know the peace.</ns0:note> to know how Esther did, and what should become of her.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Now when every maids turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus; after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Who were kept so long, partly for their better purification, as it here follows; partly out of state, as that which became so great a King, & partly that being so long in safe custody, the King might be sure that the Child<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> begotten upon any of them was his own.</ns0:note>, for so were the days of their purifications accomplished, <ns0:hi>to wit,</ns0:hi> six months with oil of myrrhe <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which is useful both for making the skin exactly clean<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and smooth and solid, and for giving strength and vigour to the body.</ns0:note>, and six months with sweet odours <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which was the more necessary, because the bodies of men and women in those hot Countries, did of themselves yield very ill scents, if not corrected and qualified by art.</ns0:note>, and with <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> things for the puri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fying of the women.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then thus <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Thus</ns0:hi> purified and prepared; and <ns0:hi>thus</ns0:hi> as it follows.</ns0:note> came every maiden unto the king; whatsoever she desired <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For ornament, or by way of attendance.</ns0:note> was given her, to go with her out of the house of the women, unto the kings house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the kings chamberlain, which kept the concubines <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Whereof <ns0:hi>Darius Nothus</ns0:hi> is reckoned to have had 360.</ns0:note>: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai (who had taken her for his daughter) was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To shew that she was not desirous to please the King, and that she was brought to the King without, and against her own inclina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion and choice.</ns0:note>, but what Hegai the kings cham<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />berlain, the keeper of the women appointed: and Est<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />her obtained favour in the sight of all them that look<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed upon her <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Was admired by them for her beauty.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 So Esther was taken unto king Ahasuerus, into his house royal <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And into his bed, as is implied. To which it is not strange, if she, though a vertuous person, did in those circumstances yield, considering the infirmity of humane nature, and of that sex, and the state of those times, when plurality of Wives were permitted, and Concubines were owned as Wives; and these Virgins were by this action made his Wives or Concubines. Besides it is not known to us whether <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> had not direction or a dispensati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on from God in this matter; it being certain that God can dispense with his own positive laws.</ns0:note>, in the tenth month (which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the month Tebeth) in the seventh year of his reign.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> kindness.</ns0:note> favour <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>before him.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> in his sight, more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> Esthers feast, and he made a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>rest.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> release to the provinces <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He took off a good part of those heavy taxes which the Persian Kings laid upon their people.</ns0:note>, and gave gifts ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the state of the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And when the virgins were gathered together the second time <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either 1. When <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> with others were brought to the Kings house as it was decreed above. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2, 3. which is called <ns0:hi>the second time,</ns0:hi> because they had taken this course once before when <ns0:hi>Vashti</ns0:hi> was chosen Queen; But there is no mention of any such former use; and by the manner of proposing, it seems to have been a new project. Or, 2. Since <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> was decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red Queen; for though that point was determined, the the Kings lust was not yet satisfied, and therefore being pleased with the for mer experiment, he desired another collection of Vir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gins whom he might make his Concubines. And this seems best to agree with the following words. For it is not probable that <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi> sate at the kings gate till <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> was Queen: for till then he only <ns0:hi>walked before the court of the womens house,</ns0:hi> as is expressed. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11.</ns0:note>, then Mordecai sat in the kings gate <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either 1.
